stages.title: Shakespearean tragedies
stages.hook: Why do audiences return to stories where the hero is doomed? What do we gain from watching a downfall?
explain: Shakespearean tragedy follows a person of high standing whose choices and flaws, in a hostile world, bring suffering and loss. The hero's tragic flaw (hamartia) might be ambition, jealousy, pride or indecision. We feel pity because the hero is human and fear because we recognise our own weakness.

Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, is told by a ghost that his father was murdered, and he struggles with doubt and delay. Macbeth, a Scottish nobleman, is spurred by a prophecy and his own ambition to seize the crown, and is destroyed by guilt. Othello, a respected general, is led by the schemer Iago to believe a false story and ruins what he loves. King Lear divides his kingdom by flattery and learns too late who truly loves him. Romeo and Juliet are young people from feuding families in Verona whose love is lost to the feud.
Tragedies often end in sorrow but also in restored order and understanding. Soliloquies let the audience see how choices are made, and imagery builds mood, for example blood in Macbeth.

example.q: Match flaw to hero: ambition and a prophecy lead to a crown by wrong means.
steps: Which play begins with a prophecy from three witches?

analogies.city: A leader who ignores honest advice may fall, like Lear.
analogies.sport: A star who lets pride overtake teamwork may fail.

stages.title: Shakespearean comedies
stages.hook: Mistaken identities, disguises and a forest where rules melt: why do comedies end with weddings?
explain: Shakespearean comedy usually follows young lovers who face obstacles such as disapproving parents, disguise or misunderstanding, and ends with harmony, often marriage. Laughter comes from wordplay, mistaken identity and the gap between what characters and audience know.

A Midsummer Night's Dream mixes four lovers lost in an Athenian wood with the fairy king Oberon and the mischievous Puck. Twelfth Night has Viola, shipwrecked in Illyria, disguised as Cesario. Much Ado About Nothing pairs the witty Beatrice and Benedick. As You Like It sends Rosalind into the Forest of Arden in disguise. The Comedy of Errors, his shortest play, depends on two sets of twins.

The Merchant of Venice is classed as a comedy but contains a harsh portrayal of the moneylender Shylock; it has been read very differently over time, and many readers see it as raising questions about prejudice and mercy.

stages.title: Shakespearean history plays
stages.hook: Does a play about kings tell us what happened, or what a playwright wanted us to believe?
explain: Shakespeare's history plays dramatise English kings. Richard II shows a king who loses his crown. Henry IV (two parts) follows young Prince Hal and the comic knight Falstaff, with Hal growing into responsibility. Henry V shows Hal as king leading England to victory at Agincourt in 1415. Richard III shows a scheming king in the Wars of the Roses. The Henry VI plays cover the lead-up.

The plays are not exact history. Shakespeare shortened events, invented speeches and shaped characters for dramatic effect. He drew on chroniclers such as Raphael Holinshed. Because he wrote under the Tudor monarchs, his portrayal of Richard III as a villain is often seen as influenced by the Tudor view and is debated by historians.
Common themes are the nature of kingship, legitimacy, loyalty and the cost of war. The famous speech in Henry V, "We few, we happy few, we band of brothers", shows how rhetoric inspires soldiers.

example.q: Place the plays: who is the king at Agincourt in Shakespeare?

analogies.city: Statues and monuments shape how we remember rulers.
analogies.sport: A commentator's account shapes who we think played best.

stages.title: Shakespearean sonnets
stages.hook: Fourteen lines to argue, praise, doubt or mourn: how does a sonnet pack so much in?
explain: Shakespeare published 154 sonnets in 1609. Each is 14 lines of iambic pentameter in the form ABAB CDCD EFEF GG: three quatrains (four-line units) and a closing couplet. Often there is a volta, a turn in thought, usually near line 9 or in the couplet.
The Italian or Petrarchan sonnet, by contrast, has an octave (8 lines) and sestet (6 lines) with a rhyme such as ABBAABBA. Shakespeare's sonnets explore love, time, beauty, jealousy and mortality.

Sonnet 18 begins "Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?" and argues that the verse will keep the subject's beauty alive. Sonnet 116 begins "Let me not to the marriage of true minds / Admit impediments" and describes love as constant. Sonnet 130 begins "My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun" and mocks exaggerated love poetry while still affirming real affection.

stages.title: Literary symbolism
stages.hook: A dove, a green light, a white whale: how can an object mean more than itself?
explain: A symbol is an object, person, colour or action that stands for a larger idea. A dove often suggests peace, a road a life journey, light hope or knowledge. In Macbeth, blood and hands that cannot be washed clean become symbols of guilt.

Symbols work through association and context. The same image may mean different things in different cultures: white may suggest purity in one tradition and mourning in another. In Herman Melville's Moby-Dick, the white whale takes on many possible meanings for readers, and in F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby, the green light across the bay suggests longing for an unreachable dream.

An allegory is an extended symbolic story, in which characters and events stand for ideas. John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress is a Christian allegory of life as a journey. George Orwell's Animal Farm uses farm animals to represent the Russian Revolution and its aftermath.

stages.title: Character and thematic analysis
stages.hook: Two readers read the same scene. One calls the character cruel, one calls her brave. How can you argue a case from the text?
explain: Literary analysis builds a claim about a text and supports it with evidence. A common method is point, evidence, explanation: make a point, quote or refer to the text, then explain how it supports the point.

Characters can be analysed by what they say, do, think and how others speak of them. A protagonist is the main character; an antagonist opposes them. A foil is a character who contrasts with another to highlight qualities. A round character is complex and can change; a flat character has one main trait. A dynamic character changes; a static one does not.

Themes emerge from patterns: conflicts, repeated images and how characters change. Strong analysis also considers context (when and where a text was written), form (poem, play or novel) and language. A good thesis is arguable, not just a summary.

stages.title: European classical literature
stages.hook: Why do writers still borrow from works that are two thousand years old?
explain: The Iliad and the Odyssey are Greek epics attributed to Homer, composed in oral tradition and written down about the 8th century BCE. The Iliad is about the anger of Achilles in the Trojan War. The Odyssey follows Odysseus's long journey home. The Roman poet Virgil wrote the Aeneid, about Aeneas, a Trojan refugee, as a founding story for Rome.

In the Middle Ages, Dante Alighieri wrote the Divine Comedy around 1320, a journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise. Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales (late 14th century) is a set of stories told by pilgrims, written in English. Miguel de Cervantes's Don Quixote (1605, 1615) follows a man who reads too many chivalry tales and sets out as a knight.

Later classics include Goethe's Faust (Germany), Molière's comedies (France), and the great Russian novels of Tolstoy and Dostoevsky. Classical works shaped later writers by giving them models, characters and themes to rework.

teach.model: Homer's Iliad and Odyssey are Greek epics. Virgil wrote the Aeneid for Rome. Dante wrote the Divine Comedy. Chaucer wrote the Canterbury Tales. Cervantes wrote Don Quixote.

stages.title: African and Asian literary classics
stages.hook: Which writers carried African and Asian stories to readers all over the world?
explain: Africa: Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart (1958) shows Igbo life in Nigeria before and during colonial arrival; it is among the most widely read African novels. Wole Soyinka of Nigeria was the first African Nobel laureate in Literature (1986) and Naguib Mahfouz of Egypt won it in 1988. Earlier, the Epic of Sundiata lived in oral performance.

Asia: Rabindranath Tagore of Bengal won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913, the first non-European winner. Kalidasa wrote Sanskrit drama such as Shakuntala. Rumi's Persian poetry of the 13th century is read worldwide. In China, Cao Xueqin's Dream of the Red Chamber (18th century) is a masterpiece of the novel, and poets Li Bai and Du Fu of the Tang dynasty are celebrated. Japan's Murasaki Shikibu and Bashō have already shaped world literature.
Many of these works are read in translation, which means a translator makes choices about meaning, sound and tone.

example.q: Place the Nobel firsts: who was the first African laureate in Literature?
steps: Nobel prizes are given each year.
He was the first from Africa.

misc.right: They wrote about universal human themes as well as local life.

stages.limits: Prizes and canons reflect particular judges and times, and many great writers have not won them.

stages.title: North American, South American and Oceanian literature
stages.hook: What did writers of the new world do with old forms: invent new ones, or blend voices?
explain: North America: Walt Whitman's Leaves of Grass (1855) broke with tradition through free verse and a wide-ranging American voice. Emily Dickinson wrote short, intense poems with dashes. Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884) used vernacular speech. Toni Morrison (Nobel Prize 1993) wrote novels of African American history and memory.

South America: Gabriel García Márquez of Colombia popularised magical realism in One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967), blending the fantastic into everyday life. Jorge Luis Borges of Argentina wrote short stories of labyrinths and libraries. Pablo Neruda of Chile wrote love poems and odes. Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz was a 17th-century Mexican poet and thinker. Machado de Assis shaped Brazilian fiction.

Oceania: Patrick White won Australia's only Nobel Prize in Literature (1973). Katherine Mansfield, from New Zealand, wrote modern short stories. Oodgeroo Noonuccal, an Aboriginal poet and activist, published We Are Going (1964), the first book of poetry by an Aboriginal Australian. Witi Ihimaera is a Māori novelist.

steps: Magical events are treated as normal.
example.a: The fantastic woven into the ordinary.

analogies.home: Family stories that include dreams and ghosts told as simple facts.
analogies.city: Writers capture voices of city streets, as Twain did river talk.
analogies.music: Poetry in the Americas often draws on song and speech rhythms.

panel.q: Explain how a writer from the Americas or Oceania might blend oral and written traditions.
panel.model: They may bring the rhythms and tales of spoken tradition into poems and novels, so written work carries the voice of oral culture.

teach.topic: North American, South American and Oceanian literature
teach.model: Whitman and Dickinson changed American poetry. Márquez made magical realism famous. Borges and Neruda wrote from South America. In Oceania, Oodgeroo Noonuccal, Patrick White and Katherine Mansfield are major voices.
